description: Sportsmanship vs gamesmanship, etiquette in action, and how spectators can help or harm sport.
content_html:
What Is Etiquette in Sport?

Etiquette refers to the expected standards of behaviour in sport that go beyond the written rules. While rules tell players what they must do, etiquette tells them what they should do to show respect for the sport, opponents, officials and spectators. Etiquette varies between sports but always promotes fair and respectful participation.

Common examples of etiquette include shaking hands with opponents after a match, applauding good play by the opposition, walking off the pitch when injured without making a fuss, and accepting the referee’s decision without argument. In tennis, players wait for a break in play before retrieving an errant ball rather than disrupting a point. In cricket, a fielder tells the umpire honestly if they grounded a catch.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in sport. It includes acts like shaking hands after a game, applauding the opposition, and kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured — all gestures that show respect without being required by the rules.

Sportsmanship vs Gamesmanship

Sportsmanship means playing within the written rules AND the spirit of the sport. A player demonstrating sportsmanship competes hard but never at the expense of fairness or respect. Sporting behaviour includes playing to win within the rules, showing respect to the referee even when you disagree, and putting the welfare of an injured opponent above the advantage of the game.

Gamesmanship, by contrast, involves bending the spirit of the rules to gain a competitive edge — without breaking them outright. A football player taking a long time over a throw-in to waste a few seconds is using gamesmanship. So is a tennis player taking unusually long between serves to disrupt an opponent’s rhythm, or a cricketer deliberately moving in a fielder’s line of sight just before a delivery.

Many students confuse these two terms. Remember: sportsmanship is doing the right thing even when the rules do not force you to. Gamesmanship is doing something that is technically legal but goes against the spirit of the sport. A handy paired example to remember: kicking the ball out of play for an injured opponent (sportsmanship) versus slowing down a throw-in to waste time (gamesmanship). The question will often ask for “one applied example of each” — always give a specific sporting situation, not a vague description.

Values That Underpin Sporting Behaviour

Sporting behaviour is underpinned by shared values that sport is meant to promote. Fair play is the idea that competition should be decided by ability and effort, not by cheating. Respect means treating opponents, officials and teammates with dignity. Tolerance means accepting differences — in skill level, background or playing style — without hostility. These values explain why etiquette and sportsmanship matter beyond any single match: they preserve sport as a positive experience for everyone involved.

Key Fact

Sportsmanship requires playing within both the letter of the rules (what is written) and the spirit of the rules (what the sport is meant to stand for). Gamesmanship only respects the letter — it exploits gaps in the rules for personal gain.

Spectator Behaviour

Spectators play a major role in the atmosphere of any sporting event. Positive spectator behaviour includes cheering your team, applauding great play from either side, staying within designated areas, and following ground regulations. These behaviours create an enjoyable and safe environment for everyone — athletes, officials and fellow spectators.

Negative spectator behaviour, however, can have serious consequences. Hooliganism refers to disorderly or violent behaviour by fans. This can include fighting in and around stadiums, chanting abuse, throwing objects onto the pitch, or invading the playing surface. Hooliganism puts players, officials and other fans at risk. It can also lead to matches being abandoned, grounds being closed and the sport’s reputation being damaged.

Following the Hillsborough disaster in 1989 — where 97 Liverpool supporters lost their lives in a crowd crush — Lord Justice Taylor produced the Taylor Report (1990). Its central recommendation was that top-flight football grounds in England should become all-seater stadia, replacing terraces where standing spectators could become dangerously compressed. By 1994–95, all Premier League and First Division grounds had converted. All-seater stadia give every fan an assigned seat, reduce crowd surges, and allow stewards to monitor and remove individuals causing problems more easily. They are now considered an essential safety standard in modern football.

The shift to all-seater grounds also changed the culture of watching football. Individual ticketing reduced the anonymity that could mask troublemakers, and CCTV coverage became far easier to implement. Crowd segregation — separating home and away supporters — was formalised. Together, these measures contributed to a significant fall in football-related disorder from the 1990s onwards.

Spectators’ Responsibilities

Spectators are not passive bystanders. They have responsibilities to the performers, to officials, and to each other. Accepting referee decisions without confronting officials, avoiding language or actions that intimidate players, and not engaging in discriminatory chanting are all expectations placed on spectators. Ground regulations typically prohibit entering the field of play, and spectators can be ejected or banned for breaking these rules.

Some stadiums use “ultras” — highly organised and passionate fan groups, typically associated with European football. While many ultras create spectacular displays using flags, banners and coordinated chanting, the culture has at times been linked to disorder. The key distinction for the exam is between passionate support (acceptable) and threatening or violent behaviour (unacceptable and illegal).

Poor spectator behaviour has direct consequences: events can be cancelled or moved, clubs can be fined or have grounds closed, international reputations suffer, and broadcasters can lose confidence in covering the sport. On the other hand, a vocal and well-behaved crowd enhances the experience for everyone, creates a positive atmosphere and encourages participation. Examiners often ask students to explain how spectator behaviour can affect the sport as a whole — think about impact on the game, the club, the players and the wider image of sport.
exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often use command words like “describe” or “explain.” When asked to describe an example of sportsmanship or gamesmanship, always name a specific sporting situation — not just “a player was respectful.” For a ‘6 marks — Discuss’ question on spectator behaviour, you must cover more than one point of view: consider the impact on players, officials, other spectators and the sport’s reputation. A common mistake is writing only about safety risks and forgetting the reputational and financial consequences of poor spectator behaviour. Always finish a discuss answer by linking points together, not just listing them.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in sport — acts like shaking hands and applauding opponents show respect beyond what the rules require.
  • Sportsmanship means honouring both the letter and the spirit of the sport; gamesmanship exploits loopholes without breaking rules. They are not the same thing.
  • Spectators have responsibilities too — hooliganism damages sport’s image and safety. The Taylor Report (1990) led to all-seater stadia in English football as a direct response to crowd disasters.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of sportsmanship?
A) A basketball player deliberately elbowing an opponent when the referee is not looking
B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment
C) A tennis player bouncing the ball unusually slowly to unsettle a nervous opponent before serving
D) A rugby player disputing every decision made by the referee throughout the match
practice_questions.marks: B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two examples of negative spectator behaviour at a live sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each genuinely distinct example (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
- Throwing objects onto the pitch / at players or officials
- Pitch invasion / entering the field of play without permission
- Racist or abusive chanting directed at players
- Fighting between rival supporters
- Using pyrotechnics (flares, smoke bombs) in the crowd
- Verbally intimidating officials or players
Do not award a second mark if both answers are essentially the same point (e.g. 'shouting abuse' and 'chanting abuse').

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between sportsmanship and gamesmanship. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a clear definition of sportsmanship (playing within the letter and spirit of the rules / showing respect for the sport and opponents). Award 1 mark for a clear definition or description of gamesmanship (bending the rules / exploiting loopholes without technically breaking them). Award 1 mark for a relevant, applied example of each:
- Sportsmanship example: e.g. kicking the ball out for an injured player; shaking hands after a defeat; accepting a referee's call without complaint
- Gamesmanship example: e.g. time-wasting at a throw-in; bouncing the ball slowly before a serve; calling an injury to disrupt opposition momentum
All 3 marks can be awarded without mentioning both examples if the definitions are sufficiently precise and applied.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which poor spectator behaviour can negatively affect a sporting event. Give one example from sport to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct negative effects (up to 2 marks each) with development:
- Safety risks: fans may be injured or killed (e.g. crowd crushes, fighting). Reference to Hillsborough 1989 or similar crowd disaster is creditworthy.
- Match disruption / abandonment: incidents of pitch invasion, flares or serious fighting may force officials to stop play.
- Reputational damage: the sport or club is associated with disorder, deterring families, sponsors and broadcasters.
- Financial penalty: governing bodies can fine clubs, close grounds or impose points deductions following crowd trouble.
A named sporting example is required for the top marks on the second point. A generic answer with no named example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Kingsmere FC is a non-league football club in Worcestershire. After a closely contested local derby, a group of away supporters entered the pitch and confronted home players. The club received a warning from the county FA.

Discuss how spectator behaviour, both positive and negative, can affect a football club like Kingsmere FC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion covering both positive and negative spectator behaviour, with development of at least two distinct effects in each direction. Points are linked and interact (e.g. one negative consequence leads to another). Named or applied examples used. Judgement or synthesis attempted.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two effects discussed, one positive and one negative, with some development beyond a simple list. Limited interaction between points.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid effects stated but with little development. May be one-sided (only positives or only negatives).

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about spectator behaviour with no development.

Credit points such as: positive atmosphere lifts player performance; community identity and belonging; negative behaviour leads to fines, ground closures, point deductions; physical safety risks; reputational damage to club and sport; impact on sponsorship and media coverage.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of etiquette that might be observed in any sport of your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct and relevant etiquette example (maximum 2 marks). Answers must name or clearly describe a specific expected behaviour rather than a vague statement. Acceptable examples:
- Shaking hands with opponents / officials after a match
- Applauding good play by the opposing team or player
- Acknowledging when a ball was out that was called in (e.g. tennis)
- Kicking the ball out for an injured opponent in football
- Walking off the field promptly when given out in cricket
- Waiting for a break in play before collecting a stray ball (tennis / badminton)
Do not award if both examples are essentially the same behaviour described differently.

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes bending the spirit of the rules to gain an advantage, without technically breaking them?
What was the main safety recommendation of the Taylor Report (1990) following the Hillsborough disaster?
options: All football clubs should install CCTV cameras
Away supporters should be banned from grounds
Top-flight football grounds should become all-seater stadia
Matches should always have police officers on the pitch

knowledge_checks.q: Etiquette in sport refers to the _____ code of behaviour expected of participants, beyond what the written rules require.
_____ means playing within both the letter and the spirit of the sport, showing respect for opponents, officials and the game.
Match each behaviour to the correct category.
left: Kicking the ball out for an injured opponent
Time-wasting at a throw-in to run down the clock
Throwing objects onto the pitch during a match

flashcard_questions.a: The unwritten code of conduct expected of performers, beyond what the rules strictly require.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of etiquette in football.
flashcard_questions.a: Kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured, then returning possession.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the principle Sportsmanship requires beyond just following the rules.
flashcard_questions.a: Playing within the spirit of the game.
Using legal tactics that bend the spirit of the rules to gain a competitive advantage.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of gamesmanship in tennis.
flashcard_questions.a: Bouncing the ball unusually slowly before serving to disrupt an opponent's concentration.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hooliganism in the context of spectator sport?
flashcard_questions.a: Violent, aggressive or criminal behaviour by fans, including fighting, pitch invasion or throwing objects.

flashcard_questions.q: What disaster in 1989 led to the Taylor Report?
flashcard_questions.a: The Hillsborough disaster, where 97 Liverpool supporters died in a crowd crush.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the key recommendation of the Taylor Report (1990)?
flashcard_questions.a: Top-flight English football grounds should convert to all-seater stadia.

flashcard_questions.q: By which season did all Premier League grounds become all-seater?
Name two values that underpin good sporting behaviour.
flashcard_questions.a: Fair play and respect. (Also accept: tolerance.)

flashcard_questions.q: How can poor spectator behaviour damage a football club financially?
flashcard_questions.a: Governing bodies can fine clubs, close grounds or impose points deductions.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes highly organised, passionate fan groups common in European football?

glossary_terms.definition: The unwritten code of behaviour that participants are expected to follow in a sport, beyond what the rules strictly require.
Behaviour that upholds both the letter and the spirit of the sport, showing respect for opponents, officials and the game itself.
Using tactics that bend the rules or exploit loopholes to gain an advantage, without technically breaking them.
Violent, aggressive or criminal behaviour by sports spectators, including fighting, pitch invasion, racist abuse or throwing objects.
